questions.prompt: A CG stage has \(g_m = 2\ \mathrm{mS}\) and very large \(r_o\). What input resistance (Ω) does its source present?
questions.explanation: With the gate at AC ground, a test voltage \(v\) at the source gives \(v_{gs} = -v\), so the device draws \(g_mv\): \(R_{in} = 1/g_m = 500\ \Omega\) (reader Eq. 12.13).

questions.prompt: Include \(r_o\): a CG stage has \(g_m = 1\ \mathrm{mS}\), \(r_o = 20\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) and \(R_D = 20\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\). Find \(R_{in}\) in kΩ.
questions.explanation: \(R_{in} = (r_o + R_D)/(1 + g_mr_o) = 40/21 = 1.90\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) (Eq. 12.10). \(1/g_m = 1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) is only valid when \(r_o \gg R_D\).

questions.prompt: What is the CG stage's short-circuit current gain \(i_{out}/i_{in}\)?
options: About 1: it passes the input current to a high-impedance output
questions.explanation: The current into the source leaves through the drain (Eq. 12.5). It works as a current buffer: low \(R_{in}\), high \(R_{out}\).

questions.prompt: Why is the CG input resistance so low?

Because \(R_D\) is in series with the input
Because the bias source shorts it
questions.explanation: The device acts as a conductance \(g_m\) at its own source. That is ideal for a current input.
